narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 54.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly more likely than passing, but it was enough for the prediction to be treated as a failure risk and for your application to be rejected.

The strongest factor was your LSAT score. At 25.50, it is well below the average of 37.18 among accepted students, and this was the main reason the prediction moved toward failure. The second most influential factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 2.80 it is below the accepted-student average of 3.23, yet in this prediction it was the one top factor that leaned toward passing rather than failing; it helped your case but could not offset the other concerns. The third factor was your third-year class rank: you were in the third decile, compared with an average of about the sixth decile for accepted students, and this pushed the prediction toward failure.

To improve a future application, focus on the areas that most affected this decision: prepare to retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, strengthen your academic record through additional coursework or a graduate credential, and seek advising on how to improve or explain your third-year performance. Consider gaining relevant legal or professional experience and reapplying once these signals are stronger.
